_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Benefit of discretion: a small matter. And if a priest gave a sela so that [the owner] would give it to another priest, his relative, it is forbidden: since [the teruma] is fit for [that priest] himself, he looks like a priest who assists [at the threshing floor].
gershom:a1.1: Benefit of discretion: that he may give it to any priest he wishes and receive a small thing for it, as it says: How so? An Israelite, etc.
gershom:a2.1: If a priest to a priest: that is, if the one who gives him the sela in order to secure it for another priest was himself a priest, it is forbidden, for it looks as though [the owner] is selling it to that priest for that sela, and he is like a priest who assists at the threshing floors. [The printed text is garbled here; this follows the editor’s correction.]
rashi:a3.1: This is the reading: “And the tanna, what is the reason he does not state the gifts of the priesthood?” And we do not read “and the first tanna.” [The baraita said:] “And in all of them there is benefit of discretion,” and explained it: for example, an Israelite who separated teruma from his pile. What is the reason he did not also say: or a butcher who separated his [priestly] gifts, or a shepherd who had firstborn animals?
gershom:a3.1: And the first tanna, who said “one does not give them teruma or tithe as their wages, and if they did so, they desecrated it”: what is the reason he did not say [this of the] gifts too? It says “the first tanna” because the one who says “And the Sages wished to penalize them,” etc., is another tanna. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “the first tanna,” the reading Rashi rejects.]
rashi:a3.2: He could have said to you, teruma: this is the reason its benefit of discretion is permitted: because it has inherent sanctity, everyone knows that it never goes out to non-sacred status. So this priest, for whose sake his mother’s father gave the sela, will not come to err and treat it as non-sacred, saying that it was redeemed by this sela that his mother’s father gave.
rashi:a4.1: But these: the [priestly] gifts [and the] firstborn.
rashi:a4.2: Since they have sanctity that inheres in their value: for if the priest wishes to sell the meat of a firstborn, or the foreleg, jaw and maw, he may sell them to an Israelite, and then the Israelite need no longer eat them roasted and with mustard as the priest does. Therefore this priest will come to err with them and think: since they can be bought and sold, …
rashi:a4.3: … their sanctity is redeemed with four zuz: that his mother’s father gave, that is, four zuz [one sela]; and he will come to treat them as non-sacred, not eating them roasted and with mustard as their law requires, as explained in the chapter HaZero’a VeHaLeḥayayim VeHaKeiva (Ḥullin 132b). And for this reason [the baraita] did not teach them. And what it said, “And in all of them,” means this: and in all of them, the terumot and the tithes, there is benefit of discretion.
gershom:a4.1: He could have said to you: since it is not redeemed, for teruma never has redemption to take it out to non-sacred status, [the priest] will not come to err with it; even though we say here “they desecrated it,” the priest will not come to treat it lightly and eat it in impurity. But these gifts, since their sanctity inheres in their value and they can be redeemed, if I were to say “they desecrated it,” he would come to err with them and treat them with the disregard shown to non-sacred food, and perhaps feed them to dogs, which would be a disgrace. [On Rava’s statement that follows:] It does not have [any prohibition] due to a priest, etc.: because it is not so stringent.
tosafot:a4.1: And he will come to treat them as non-sacred: and we require (Zevaḥim 28a) [that they be eaten] “for greatness,” in the way kings eat, roasted and with mustard. And with all the gifts it is written “for greatness,” even the foreleg, the jaw and the maw, as is implied here. But regarding teruma we do not find that any eating requires [the manner of] greatness; perhaps greatness applies only to meat.
rashi:a5.1: Teruma from outside the Land: is rabbinic, and one may give it to a priest who assists.
rashi:a5.2: To his servant: [who was] a priest.
gershom:a5.1: He gave it to his servant: a priest, as his wages, and he was not concerned that [the servant] would look like [a priest] who assists.
rashi:a6.1: Is nullified in a majority: so that a non-priest may eat it, and we do not require one in a hundred. And after one has mixed it into a majority of non-sacred produce, a non-priest may eat it, or a priest in his days of impurity, once he has nullified it.
tosafot:a6.1: Teruma from outside the Land is nullified in a majority: this means [nullified] to permit it to an impure priest, as it says: Rabba would nullify it in a majority [and eat it] in his days of impurity. It is not as the Kuntres [Rashi] explained, that a non-priest may eat it and one in a hundred is not required. For it is proven explicitly in Menaḥot, chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Menaḥot 67a), that they are forbidden to a non-priest: [the mishna there teaches that] regarding a gentile’s ḥalla in the Land and his teruma outside the Land, one informs him that he is exempt; his ḥalla is eaten by non-priests and his teruma does not create a forbidden mixture. And [the Gemara] infers there: but that of a Jew does create a forbidden mixture, which implies that it does not become permitted to non-priests unless [it is nullified] in one hundred and one.
rashi:a6.2: Rabba: was a priest, for he descended from the house of Eli.
tosafot:a6.2: Rabba would nullify it in a majority, etc.: the reading is Rabba, who was a priest, as we say that Rabba descended from the house of Eli. But Rava was not a priest, as is proven in the chapter HaZero’a (Ḥullin 133a), where Rava said to his servant: Acquire the gifts for me, etc.
gershom:a6.1: He would nullify it in a majority: one in two, and one in a hundred is not required as with teruma of the Land.
gershom:a7.1: And eat it: even an Israelite [may eat it], in days of impurity, like non-sacred food. And Rabba was a priest.
rashi:a7.1: Teruma wine: from outside the Land.
gershom:a8.1: And Rav Huna too [would do so]: he would pour two jugs of non-sacred wine and one of teruma, take out one and drink it. From then on he would pour one of teruma into those two jugs and take out one, and so he would do until all the teruma was used up, nullifying it in this way.
rashi:a8.1: He proceeds to eat: the untithed produce, and leaves over enough for the teruma, and separates it at the end.
tosafot:a8.1: He proceeds to eat and afterward separates: this implies that [the teruma] need not be [separated from produce] adjacent [to the rest]. But I could explain that at the very end, after he separates the teruma, some of his pile would remain, so that the requirement of adjacency would be fulfilled. The Kuntres [Rashi], however, explained: he proceeds to eat and leaves over enough for the teruma, and separates it at the end.
gershom:a9.1: And afterward separate: even at the end.
rashi:a9.1: Impurity that comes from his body: for example, a zav, a zava, a menstruating woman, or one who had a seminal emission. But to one impure from a corpse it is permitted.
gershom:a10.1: One whose impurity comes from his body: for example, a zav or one who had a seminal emission.
rashi:a9.2: With regard to touching, we have no problem with it: and even though he renders it impure, we do not mind, since he is not warned to guard it from becoming impure.
gershom:a11.1: But with regard to touching, we have no problem with it: even one whose impurity comes from his body may touch it.
rashi:a10.1: Therefore: since one is not warned about touching, a menstruating woman cuts off ḥalla [from her dough] and [a minor priest] eats it.
rashi:a10.2: A minor priest: and not an adult, because [for him] impurity has come from his body; but if he immersed for his seminal emission, he is like a minor. Another version: it specifies a minor priest because he has not had a seminal emission and no impurity has come from his body. And in the She’iltot of Rav Aḥai it is explained this way.
tosafot:a10.1: Therefore a menstruating woman separates ḥalla and a minor priest eats it: it is somewhat puzzling why it specifies a minor priest, since even an adult may eat it after he immerses and is purified of his seminal emission. And if it is because of the trouble of immersing, in the Land too they immerse for teruma, and in Babylonia too they would immerse for teruma from outside the Land, as is implied above, that Rabba ate it [nullified] in a majority only in his days of impurity; and at the beginning of [the chapter] Benot Kutim (Niddah 32a), where they immersed [a girl] before her mother [so that she could be anointed] with teruma oil. From this the Ri concludes that this ḥalla has no fixed measure, and since it is a small amount, she gives it to a minor priest. The wording “she takes it with the top of a skewer” also implies that it is a small amount. And although this is mentioned only regarding the burning, it still implies that the one given to the minor is also a small amount; and the one that is burned had to be described “with the top of a skewer” because with it she throws it into the oven. But their teruma, which was of grain, was not so fit to be given to a minor priest even if it had no fixed measure, since a minor would waste it; and the same for wine and oil. Alternatively, one may say that teruma has a fixed measure, for example the teruma of the tithe.
gershom:a12.1: Therefore a menstruating woman separates ḥalla: outside the Land; for with a menstruating woman too, her impurity comes from her body.
gershom:a13.1: And a minor priest eats it: for impurity does not come from his body. And this ḥalla that we learned here, that a minor priest eats, meaning that it is forbidden to one whose impurity comes from his body, is all taught about the ḥalla for the fire. For nowadays we give two ḥallot, one for the fire and one for the priest. The one for the fire has no fixed measure and the priest’s has a fixed measure. The one for the fire is teruma by Torah law, and for this reason we throw it into the fire, since we cannot give it to a priest, because outside the Land is presumed impure and is like a beit haperas [a field in which a grave was plowed up]. Therefore we give it to the fire, and the one we give to the priest is so that the law of ḥalla not be forgotten from Israel. And so it stands to reason that this case concerns the [ḥalla] for the fire, for if it were the priest’s, why would one need to give it to a minor priest? Even an impure priest may eat it, for so we read in tractate Ḥalla, in the last chapter, [after the mishna] about two women who made two kav: Rabban Gamliel says: There are three lands with regard to ḥalla, etc., and one who immersed that day eats it; Rabbi Yosei says: He need not immerse. [The note ends with an unclear abbreviation.]
rashi:a10.3: With the top of a skewer [massa]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). For as far as she can take care not to touch it once she has designated it [as ḥalla], she takes care.
tosafot:a10.2: With the top of a skewer and throws it in the oven: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that as far as she can take care not to touch it once she has designated it, she takes care. This is difficult for his explanation, since regarding touching they said “we have no problem with it,” and touching it is entirely permitted. Rather, it mentions the top of the skewer because one normally turns over coals and wood with it, as the Kuntres explained massa (with an Old French gloss), and with it she can put the ḥalla well into the oven, into the fire. And it seems that the massa is the baker’s peel [mardeh] with which bread is taken out [of the oven], as is implied in Ta’anit (25a) about the wife of Rabbi Ḥanina, where her neighbor said to her: Bring a massa, for your bread is burning, and we say there: she too had gone in to bring a peel. But a matara could be a poker, as the Kuntres explained in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (4b) about [Miriam] who raised children, who took the matara and was raking the oven: she was holding the oven’s poker, which is called the oven’s broom. And because there are things that become obligated in ḥalla only after baking, such as sponge cakes and honey cakes, in the chapter Kol Sha’ah (Pesaḥim 37a), and as it says, he ground, kneaded and baked it and separated ḥalla from it, it says “she takes it with the top of the massa”: when she comes to take [the bread out of the oven], she burns [the ḥalla], throwing it into the fire with the top of the peel itself.
gershom:a14.1: With the top of the massa: the first portion of the dough. [Rabbeinu Gershom apparently takes massa to mean the dough rather than a skewer.]
rashi:a10.4: An adult priest [lit. a great priest]: a priest who has reached the age of the commandments.
tosafot:a10.3: In brief: And then she separates another ḥalla: this implies that they were strict to separate a second ḥalla only where there is no minor priest, unlike the places taught in tractate Ḥalla (4:8), where one always separates two ḥallot, one for the fire and one for the priest. Those places are near the Land, and their ḥalla looks like the impure ḥalla of the Land, which must be burned; they decreed that even a fully pure priest may not eat it because it is impure, so there they always separate one for the fire and a second so that the law of ḥalla is not forgotten, as is explained here too. But here in Babylonia, far from the Land, their ḥalla does not look like the impure ḥalla of the Land and no prohibition was decreed on account of the impurity itself; so they permitted it even to an impure priest whose impurity does not come from his body, and permitted nullifying it in a majority, and the second one an adult priest may eat, even a zav, since no distinction is made here. Although the mishna there teaches that the second ḥalla is forbidden to zavim, zavot, menstruating women and women after childbirth, one cannot learn from it to forbid this one to zavim: it is in Babylonia, far from the Land, and it is separated only where there is no [minor] priest, unlike the places near the Land that always separate two. Some corrected texts say that this other ḥalla is not called ḥalla, since it has no law of ḥalla; and it stands to reason that it does not create a forbidden mixture, even though teruma from outside the Land does, as taught in Menaḥot, chapter Rabbi Yishmael; perhaps even the second ḥalla in the places listed in the mishna does not. And it seems to Rabbi [the author] that both here and there, even where they were strict to separate a second ḥalla, they were not strict to separate two terumot, since the mishna requires two only for ḥalla. A reason may be given: with ḥalla there is more concern that it be forgotten, since it applies to everyone who kneads dough, whereas teruma is common only among landowners and those who smooth piles of grain. rashi:a11.1: [To relieve himself: lit. “to the openings,” i.e., to the privy. This gloss is printed in brackets.]
rashi:a11.2: May he immerse and eat teruma from outside the Land: without waiting for sunset.
rashi:b1.1: But do we have sprinkling: nowadays? Since there is no sprinkling nowadays, waiting for sunset is not required either.
tosafot:b1.1: In brief: But do we have sprinkling? It would not seem right to say that when they became impure from a corpse they would go to the Land, be sprinkled, return and eat teruma, [on the reasoning] that the Sages disregarded only the impurity of the lands outside the Land for ḥalla from outside the Land, but forbade it for every Torah-level impurity until one immersed. It is unreasonable that they instituted a priest’s ḥalla outside the Land that he could eat only by going to the Land of Israel to be sprinkled. And corpse impurity cannot be avoided: even though priests must guard against it, they cannot guard against the impurity of a sword, which is like a corpse even through a tent (Nazir 53b; the beginning of Oholot), nor need they keep away from such impurity (the beginning of Tosefta Oholot: any corpse impurity for which a nazirite does not shave, a priest is not warned about). So it stands to reason that they ate it without sprinkling or immersion. From this one must explain the mishna in Ḥalla (4:8), “from the river to Amanah and inward, two ḥallot … one who immersed that day eats it; Rabbi Yosei says: he need not immerse”: it speaks of one who immersed for a seminal emission, who is permitted without waiting for sunset even though his impurity comes from his body, for if it spoke of corpse impurity, do we have sprinkling? And Rabbi Yosei says that even one who had an emission need not immerse; proof: the latter clause forbids it to zavim, zavot, menstruating women and women after childbirth and does not list one who had an emission (as the Yerushalmi says, that clause is needed only for Rabbi Yosei). Tosafot then explains the whole mishna: three lands for ḥalla; from Keziv to the river and to Amanah, two ḥallot, the one for the fire with a fixed measure because it is Torah law, the priest’s without one because it is rabbinic; from Amanah inward, two ḥallot, the fire’s without a measure because it is burned and the priest’s with a measure, both rabbinic (Yerushalmi). This is the mishna cited briefly in Ḥullin 104a; the Talmud often shortens or lengthens mishnayot from Zera’im and Teharot when it cites them (Pesaḥim 10a; Avoda Zara 68b with Orla 2:1, which differs from Me’ila 18a, as Rabbeinu Tam explained). “And it is given to any priest” means even a priest who is an am ha’aretz, since for teruma from outside the Land they did not decree lest he eat it in impurity, like the next mishna, which lists the foreleg, jaw, maw and first shearing; yet where there is a ḥaver one should not give it to an am ha’aretz (Ḥullin 130b), against Rashi’s explanation in Ḥullin 104b. Tosafot concludes that likewise the ḥalla for the fire in Babylonia, though forbidden to one whose impurity comes from his body, does not require waiting for sunset, though the proof is not conclusive. Halakhot Gedolot writes: “Ravina said: Therefore a menstruating woman separates ḥalla and a minor priest eats it, or one who immersed for his emission,” and that in the Land only one ḥalla is separated and it is burned. But it seems that nowadays, since it is burned because there is no sprinkling anywhere in the Land, one must separate a second one, as from Keziv to the river and Amanah, so that the law of ḥalla is not forgotten. gershom:b1.1: But do we have sprinkling: nowadays, that he would need to wait for the third and seventh days? And the halakha is not in accordance with him: for one impure from a corpse never eats teruma that is Torah law, and all of these are taught about that [ḥalla] for the fire. And likewise [the ruling about] one impure from a creeping animal is taught about teruma for the fire.
rashi:b1.2: Shouldn’t we be concerned for the old man: as an astonished question. Shall we not be concerned for the honor of Rav Amram, who is not here? It is not good to issue any ruling until he comes.
rashi:b1.3: He immerses and eats: and need not wait for sunset.
rashi:b2.1: But the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion: the Talmud responds this.
tosafot:b2.1: But the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion: in that he requires immersion; rather, even immersion is not required. And the wording of the Kuntres [Rashi] does not imply this.
gershom:b2.1: It is eaten year by year: by the priest, throughout the year of the firstborn, as explained in the Gemara, whether unblemished or blemished, in the time of the Temple, as it is said: “Before the Lord,” etc.
rashi:b3.1: That we count according to its own year: if the firstborn was born in Nisan, he may keep it until the next Nisan, and we do not say that when Tishrei comes, since the year of the world’s count is complete, the firstborn’s year is complete too.
gershom:b3.1: If a blemish developed within its year: and there is no priest there to give it to.
gershom:b4.1: He may maintain it the entire twelve months: until its year is complete, for perhaps a priest will come and take it.
gershom:b6.1: After its year: if a blemish developed in it, he is not permitted [to keep it longer]; he must maintain it only thirty days, which are considered a year, as we say in the Gemara.
gershom:b7.1: Evidently it is eaten in another year too, as it is written “year by year.” And if no priest has come within thirty days, the Israelite slaughters it, salts it and hangs it up until a priest comes and takes it; and if it rots, he buries it. [The printed edition’s editor notes that this needs explanation: why would the owners not eat it themselves before it rots, since a blemished firstborn is permitted to non-priests?]
rashi:b4.1: This is the year of the firstborn: that is, when you follow the firstborn’s year, it enters into its fellow: by the time the firstborn has had one year, a second year of the world’s count has begun from Tishrei.
tosafot:b4.1: “Year by year”: which is a year that enters its fellow? Regarding “as a hired worker year by year” (Leviticus 25:53) [we expound] that the wages of this year are paid only in the next year (Bava Metzia 65a); we expound each according to its own context. And regarding tithe, where “year by year” is written, we expound below (Bekhorot 53b) that one does not tithe from the new for the old or from the old for the new. And this discussion must be established as referring to a year without [three] festivals, since with the festivals alone [the owner] violates “do not delay” every year, as it says in the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (6b). And if you say: but [this verse] is needed for what we expound in Temura, chapter VeElu Kodashim, at its end (21b), that [the firstborn] is not disqualified from one year to the next; and Ben Azzai expounds in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (29a) and the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (6a), “the one who offers it shall not be accepted”: it is not accepted, but one who delays his vow is not [subject to] “shall not be accepted,” and two verses are required there, one for the firstborn and one for other offerings. One may answer that this discussion here follows Aḥerim there, in Zevaḥim (29a), Rosh HaShana (5b) and Temura (21b), who juxtapose the firstborn to the tithe: just as the tithe is not disqualified from one year to the next, etc. And in Temura it also says that Aḥerim apply the verse “You shall eat it year by year” to [the derivation] here, and the sages here hold like Aḥerim.
gershom:b8.1: Which is a year that enters its fellow? It is that of the firstborn: if it was born in Nisan or Iyar, we do not say that when Tishrei, the New Year, comes, its year has already passed; rather we give it twelve months from the day it was born. And this is “enters its fellow”: even though its year enters the second year of the world’s count, we follow its own year, for any twelve months count as a year here.
rashi:b5.1: One day in this year: for when one slaughters it on the last day of its year, he may eat it that day and the next day, which is in its second year; that is two days.
gershom:b9.1: This is why “year by year” is written: that one takes a day of this year and a day of that year, that is, two days; from here [we learn] that it is eaten for two days.
rashi:b6.1: And the school of Rav, from where do they derive it: that we count according to its own year?
rashi:b6.2: From sacrificial animals: from other offerings that are brought in their first year, about which it is written “a lamb in its first year.”
rashi:b7.1: “And their flesh shall be yours, as the breast of waving”: this speaks of the firstborn, in the Torah portion Koraḥ. A thanks offering is eaten only for a day and a night, and what is separated from it, namely the breast and thigh, is like it.
gershom:b10.1: And Rav: it is written at the end of the verse, “it shall be yours”; the verse added another “being” for the firstborn, that is, one day more than a thanks offering. [This is the Gemara’s answer on 28a.]
